name: Biotin
short: Biotin supplements can make some laboratory immunoassays read falsely high or low, notably thyroid tests and also troponin and hormone assays, risking misdiagnosis; the effect depends on the assay.
text: The main safety concern in the cited sources is interference with laboratory tests rather than direct toxicity: supplemental biotin can interfere with immunoassays that use biotinylated reagents, falsely raising results in competitive assays and falsely lowering them in sandwich assays. Reviews describe a falsely low TSH combined with falsely high free T4 and free T3, which can mimic an overactive thyroid, and list other susceptible tests including thyroglobulin, sex hormones, ferritin, vitamin D, vitamin B12, PSA, parathyroid hormone, troponins and digoxin measurement; the interference depends on the testing platform, and manufacturers have made assays less vulnerable. In a prospective study of 13 adults, 10 mg a day interfered with specific assays for TSH, free T4, total T3 and thyroglobulin, with the greatest interference two hours after a dose; the authors highlighted people needing careful titration of levothyroxine, such as those with thyroid cancer. One review lists informing patients before blood tests among the solutions to overcome the interference. No medicine interaction data were found in the cited sources.
